segments.translit: tam eva yathābhūtārthaṃ cāṭillapādāḥ śabdāntareṇa prakaṭayanti —
segments.translation: [Cāṭilapāda]{p-catila} makes plain that same meaning, just as it truly is, in other words:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: [Cāṭilapāda]{p-catila} makes plain, in other words, "that same" meaning, just as it truly is. He does not say which earlier teaching "that same" points back to. The Tibetan translation has "the meaning of reality (de kho na nyid) as it is" (cp.05.m1).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads "de kho na nyid kyi don ji lta ba bzhin du gyur pa'i tsA TI la'i zhabs kyis": it has de kho na nyid, "reality", where the Sanskrit has tam eva, "that same", and its gyur pa'i may attach the phrase to the poet ("Cāṭilapāda, who has become [one with] the meaning of reality as it is"). The introduction otherwise says the same thing. I translate the Sanskrit.
The manuscript spells the name cāṭillapādāḥ here (cāṭila- in cp.05.m3 and in the song). I use the glossary form Cāṭilapāda; the translit keeps the manuscript spelling.

segments.translit: bha[va]ṇai ityādi | pūrvoktalalanārasanādyābhāṣatrayaṃ pārāva[ā]ragambhīratvena nadīsandhyayā boddhavyaṃ | divārātrau ca sandhyāyāṃ viṣayollolam utpadyate vinaśyati ca | ata eva gahana[ṃ] bhayānakaṃ | prakṛtidoṣād gabhīraṃ | ṣaṭpathadvāreṇa mūtrapurīṣādikaṃ ca pravahatīti | ata eva antadvayaṃ pārāvāraṃ vāmadakṣiṇaṃ cikhilam iti prakṛtidoṣapaṅkānuliptaṃ | madhye tasyā[ḥ] thāhaṃ | avadhūtyāḥ pramāṇasvarūpaṃ kartu[ṃ] na pāryate bālayoginā |
segments.translation: "The [river]{river} of [existence]{bhava}…" and so on. The three [appearances]{abhasa} spoken of earlier, [lalanā]{lalana}, [rasanā]{rasana} and the rest, are to be understood in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} as a river, because of the depth between their near and far banks. By day, by night and at twilight a surge of [sense objects]{visaya} arises and perishes. That is why it is "fathomless", that is, terrifying. It is "deep" because of the [faults of nature]{prakrtidosa}: through the doors of the six paths flow urine, excrement and the like. That is why "[both sides]{antadvaya}", the near and far banks, [left and right]{vama-daksina}, have "[mud]{cikhila}": they are smeared with the mud of the faults of nature. "In the middle" of it, "no [footing]{thaha}": a novice [yogi]{yogi} cannot take the true measure of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [river]{river} as the three [appearances]{abhasa}, [lalanā]{lalana}, [rasanā]{rasana} and the rest, where sense objects surge and perish. Its depth is the [faults of nature]{prakrtidosa}, urine and excrement flowing out; its muddy banks are [left and right]{vama-daksina}; the middle without footing is the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, which novices cannot measure. The Tibetan calls the middle unsmeared by that mud (cp.05.m2).

equations.en: the three appearances spoken of earlier, lalanā, rasanā and the rest, called a river in twilight language
deep because of the faults of nature: urine, excrement and the like flow out through the doors of the six paths
the near and far banks, left and right
smeared with the mud of the faults of nature
the avadhūtī, whose true measure a novice yogi cannot take

flags.note: Mud. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the two sides "shin tu 'dred pa", "very slippery", for cikhila, and then "rang bzhin gyi skyon gyi 'dam gyis ma gos pa dbu ma'i don la bdag nyid de", "not stained by the mud of the faults of nature, [this is] the nature of the middle": it negates the Sanskrit anuliptaṃ, "smeared" (perhaps reading an-upaliptaṃ), and applies the phrase to the middle rather than to the two banks. I translate the Sanskrit; the note mentions the Tibetan because it changes what the mud describes.

pramāṇasvarūpaṃ kartuṃ: I take pramāṇa as "measure" (hence "take the true measure"), since it answers the song's thāha, a bottom within reach. pramāṇa can also mean "valid cognition" ("a novice cannot make the true nature of the avadhūtī an object of valid knowledge"). The Tibetan "a wa d+hU tI'i tshad ma'i rang bzhin" keeps the ambiguity, tshad ma being the usual word for both.
madhye tasyāḥ thāhaṃ has no negative: the song's na ("no footing") is carried by na pāryate, "cannot". tasyāḥ (feminine) refers to the river (nadī). The Tibetan has no lemma for thāha here.

Smaller differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): "brkyang ma dang ro ma'i rtsa'i snang ba rnams gsum", "the three appearances of the channels lalanā and rasanā", adds rtsa, "channel", and has no "and the rest"; "rnam g.yeng", "distraction", renders ullola, "surge"; gahana is rendered "klong dang bcas pa", "with eddies", as in its line 1a, before the gloss "'jigs su rung ba", "terrifying".
ṣaṭpathadvāreṇa, "through the doors of the six paths": the six are not named; bodily openings seem to be meant, but I translate literally.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena caturthānandam uddīpayann ā[ha] | dharmārthaṃ svalakṣaṇadhāraṇāt dharmaḥ ghaṭapaṭastambhakumbhādibhūtavikāraḥ | tasya svarūpeṇa nāsti rūpam iti || śrīherukatantratattvapaṭaloktavicārānupalambhatayā | cāṭilasiddhācāryaḥ | śatrumam iti saṃvṛtiparamārthayor aikyaṃ gurusampradāyāt(ya) | ghaṭayati tathā ca sarahapādāḥ ||
suṇṇa karuṇa jo puṇu johuṇa vena vikasai
ṇo bhavaṇo nivvāṇe thakkai |
ahavā kevala karuṇā bhāvai
janmasahasrem̐ mokkha na pāvai ||
anena siddhācāryopāyena mokṣotsukā ye yoginaḥ | te 'pi niyataṃ saṃsārasamudrasya pāraṃ gacchantīti |
segments.note: Munidatta says the refrain illuminates the fourth [joy]{ananda}. He takes [dharma]{dharma} as a phenomenon, like a pot: it holds its own characteristic but has no form of its own. The [bridge]{bridge} is the unity of conventional and ultimate, built through the guru's lineage; he cites Saraha on joining emptiness and compassion. By this means yogis surely cross saṃsāra (cp.05.m3).

equations.en: a phenomenon: what holds its own characteristic, a transformation of the elements such as a pot or a cloth, which has no form in its true nature

equations.src: śatrumam (apparently for saṃkramam, the song's sāṅkama)
equations.en: the unity of the conventional and the ultimate, which Cāṭila builds through the guru's lineage

citations.quoted: Whoever joins emptiness and compassion / stays neither in existence nor in nirvāṇa; / but whoever meditates on compassion alone / does not gain liberation in a thousand births.
citations.work: A dohā of Saraha (Munidatta names only the author, as Sarahapāda); perhaps from Saraha's Dohākoṣa

citations.quoted: Not a quotation: a reference to the analysis (vicāra) taught in the chapter on reality (tattvapaṭala), through which nothing is apprehended.
citations.work: Śrī Heruka Tantra, chapter on reality (tattvapaṭala), as Munidatta names it; which tantra of the Hevajra or Cakrasaṃvara cycle is meant is uncertain

flags.note: śatrumam makes no sense in context. I read it as a corruption of saṃkramam, "bridge" (the song's sāṅkama, and Munidatta's own word in cp.05.m5); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) confirms with "zam pa zhes gsungs pa", "what he calls 'bridge'". The "(ya)" after gurusampradāyāt is Shastri's and does not affect the sense.

The first line of Saraha's verse is corrupt: "suṇṇa karuṇa jo puṇu johuṇa vena vikasai". "Whoever joins" is my conjecture (johuṇa as a form of "join"; vena perhaps for beṇṇa, "both"; vikasai unexplained), chosen because the second line, "ṇo bhavaṇo nivvāṇe thakkai", describes someone who stays neither in existence nor in nirvāṇa. The Tibetan reads a negative condition instead: "stong nyid snying rje dag ni sbyor ba med gyur na / srid dang myang 'das mi gnas thob par mi nus so", "if emptiness and compassion are not joined, one cannot attain the non-abiding in existence and nirvāṇa": the same teaching, stated the other way round.

śrīherukatantra…vicārānupalambhatayā stands between two sentences. I attach it to the preceding one (the dharma has no form of its own, through the non-apprehension of that analysis). The Tibetan attaches it to the following one: "…dmigs pa med pa de yis grub pa'i slob dpon tsA TI li pas zam pa zhes gsungs pa", "by that non-apprehending analysis the siddha master Cāṭilipa spoke of 'bridge'".

Last sentence: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has "grub pa'i slob dpon gyi thabs 'dis thar pa rang gi lus kyis ni rnal 'byor pas so", "by this means of the siddha master, liberation [is gained] by yogis through their own body", where the Sanskrit has mokṣotsukāḥ, "eager for liberation"; and it has only "rgya mtsho'i pha rol", "the far shore of the ocean", without saṃsāra.

The Tibetan has "nye bar 'byed par byed", "opens up, discloses", where the Sanskrit has ghaṭayati, "joins, builds" (the song's gaṭai); "bla ma'i drin gyis", "by the guru's kindness", for gurusampradāyāt, "through the guru's lineage"; and in the list of things "bum pa dang snam bu dang ka ba dang rdzas", with rdzas, "substance", where the Sanskrit has kumbha, "jar", and bhūta, "elements".
niyataṃ, "surely", seems to render the song's nibhara, so I translate it "without fail", as the draft does in 2b; pāraṃ gacchanti likewise answers pāragāmi.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇoktārthavyaktikaraṇam āha —
phāṛia ityādi | mohataruṃ viṣayaṃ vyāvṛtiva(vi)śāt tam eva saṃvṛtibodhicittavṛkṣaṃ pāṭayitvā tasya viṣayagrahaṃ khaṇḍayitvā satatālokaṃ pāṭakena saha ekīkaraṇaṃ ghaṭayati | punar asya phalapratipādanāya yuganaddhaparaśunā dṛḍhaṃ karotīti |
segments.translation: With the next [verse]{pada} he speaks, making plain the meaning already stated. "Splitting…" and so on. He splits the [tree of delusion]{mohataru}, which, because it is caught up in [sense objects]{visaya}, is that very [tree]{tree} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}; that is, he breaks up its grasping at sense objects. He joins the [constant light]{satataloka} together with the [plank]{plank}, making them one. Then, to bring about its fruit, he makes it firm with the [axe]{axe} of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [tree of delusion]{mohataru} as the tree of conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, caught up in sense objects: splitting it breaks its grasping at them. The [constant light]{satataloka} is made one with the [plank]{plank} (the Tibetan: the constant clear light is the plank), and it is made firm with the axe of coupled union, to bring about its fruit (cp.05.m4).

equations.en: that very tree of conventional bodhicitta, caught up in sense objects; splitting it breaks up its grasping at them
the plank, joined into one with the constant light (the Tibetan makes the constant clear light the plank itself)
the axe of coupled union, with which it is made firm to bring about its fruit

flags.note: mohataruṃ viṣayaṃ vyāvṛtiva(vi)śāt is doubtful. I read viṣaya- as the first member of a compound and vyāvṛti as standing for vyāpṛti, "engagement", giving "because it is caught up in sense objects", as the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) suggests: "ma rig pa'i ljon shing ni yul la 'jug pa'i dbang las de la de bzhin du kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems kyi ljon shing", "the tree of ignorance, by force of engaging with objects, is likewise the tree of conventional bodhicitta". Taken as it stands, vyāvṛti means "turning away, exclusion": "the tree of delusion, the sense object: by force of turning away, [he splits] that very tree of conventional bodhicitta".

Plank. The Tibetan has "rtag tu 'od gsal ni yang spang leb ste lhan cig tu byed pa ni yang dag bsgrigs pa'o", "the constant clear light is the plank, and making [them] one is 'properly joined'": it makes the constant light the plank itself, and has 'od gsal, "clear light" (prabhāsvara), for āloka, "light". The Sanskrit joins the constant light with the plank. The note mentions this.

The Tibetan has "ma rig pa'i ljon shing", "tree of ignorance", for mohataru, as in its line 3a; "'bras bu rtogs par bya ba'i phyir", "in order to realize the fruit", for phalapratipādanāya; and "sta re", "axe", in the comment against "gzong gnyis", "two chisels", in its line 3b.

The comment does not take up nibāṇe, "at nirvāṇa", in line 3b: "dṛḍhaṃ karoti", "makes firm", answers kohia only. The Tibetan line has "brtan par mya ngan 'das pa phug", "firmly pierced nirvāṇa", but its comment also has only "brtan par byed pa", "makes firm".

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena mārgasya anuśaṃsām āhuḥ —
sāṅkama ityādi | sthādhiṣṭhānaprabhāsvarayor aikyaṃ saṃkramaṃ jinasya sattvānāṃ saṃsārasamudrapārakaraṇāya | bho yoginaḥ | tatrārūḍhe sati vāmadakṣiṇacandrasūryābhāsau pūrvaṃ vajrajāpaṃ nirodhāt punar api paścādbhāva[ṃ] mā cintayiṣyatha | etenābhyāsavaśena bodhimahāmudrāsiddhir na dū[ra]tarā | atīva sannihiteva | tato vimārgaṃ mā yatathā dūraṃ mā gacchatha ity arthaḥ |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks in praise of the path. "Once you climb onto the [bridge]{bridge}…" and so on. The unity of [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} and [clear light]{prabhasvara} is the [bridge]{bridge} of the [Jina]{p-jina}, for carrying beings [across]{para} the ocean of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. O [yogis]{yogi}, once you have climbed onto it, do not think again, afterwards, of the [appearances]{abhasa} of the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}, [left and right]{vama-daksina}, since they have first been stopped by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}. Through the force of this practice the [accomplishment]{siddhi} of [Mahāmudrā]{mahamudra}, which is [awakening]{bodhi}, is not far off: it is, as it were, very close at hand. So do not strive on a wrong path; do not go far. That is the meaning.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [bridge]{bridge} as the unity of [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} and [clear light]{prabhasvara}, the Jina's bridge across saṃsāra. Right and left are the appearances of moon and sun: once stopped by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, they are not to be thought of again. Through this practice awakening, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, is very near; do not take a wrong path (cp.05.m5).

equations.en: the unity of self-blessing and clear light, the Jina's bridge for carrying beings across the ocean of saṃsāra
the appearances of the moon and the sun, first stopped by vajra recitation and not to be thought of again
the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which is awakening (a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss)
do not strive on a wrong path

flags.note: sthādhiṣṭhāna is evidently svādhiṣṭhāna, "self-blessing"; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has "rang byin gyis brlab pa".
vajrajāpaṃ is accusative; I construe it as instrumental ("stopped by vajra recitation"), as the Tibetan does: "rdo rje'i bzlas pas 'gog pa las".

paścādbhāvaṃ mā cintayiṣyatha: literally "do not think of a later state"; I take it as "do not think of them again afterwards", though "do not think of their coming back" is possible. The Tibetan has "slar yang phyi nas sgom pas bsam par mi bya'o", "do not think [of them] again afterwards through meditation", apparently taking bhāva as bhāvanā, "meditation".

The Tibetan translation has no word for the Jina ("skye bo sems pa rnams 'khor ba'i rgya mtsho las pha rol tu byed pa'i phyir"; sems pa is perhaps a slip for sems can, "beings"), and "shin du nye ba nyid do", "very near indeed" (nyid, as if eva), where the Sanskrit sannihiteva has iva, "as it were".
vimārgaṃ mā yatathā: I translate "do not strive on a wrong path" (yat, "strive"); the Tibetan "lam ngan pa la 'gro ba", "going on a bad path", suggests mā yātha, "do not go".
anuśaṃsā: "praise", as the Tibetan "rjes su bsngags pa" has it; in Buddhist Sanskrit the word often means "benefit, advantage" ("he speaks of the benefits of the path").

segments.translit:
yogāspadena caturthapadam āha — jai tumhetyādi | ābhāsatrayamahāmohanadyāḥ pāragamanaṃ yadīṣyate bho yoginas tadā siddhācāryopadeśapāramparyeṇānuttaradharmasvāminam āha — pṛcchatheti | ata eva sahajānandopadeśaṃ jānāmy ahaṃ niścitam iti | anyayoginas tathāvidhaṃ na jānanti | pustakadṛṣṭagarvatvāt |
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryapādair abhihitaṃ dohākoṣe —
saha ekku pava acchitahiṃ phuṛa kāhnu parijānai |
bahu savvāgama paṭai guṇai vaṭa kimpi ṇa jānai || 5 ||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of the ground of yoga. "If you…" and so on. "O [yogis]{yogi}, if you wish to go [across]{para} the [river]{river} of great [delusion]{moha} that is the three [appearances]{abhasa}, then," he says, "ask the lord of the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [Dharma]{dharma}, through the succession of the [siddha]{siddha} masters' [instruction]{upadesa}." Hence: "I know the instruction on [innate joy]{sahajananda} for certain." Other yogis do not know it in that way, because of their pride in what they have seen in books. And so [Kṛṣṇācāryapāda]{p-kanha} has said in the [Dohākoṣa]{tx-dohakosa}:
The one path, the [innate]{sahaja}, is there: [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} knows it clearly.
The lad reads and recites all the many scriptures, and knows nothing at all.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the last couplet as addressed to yogis who would cross the river of great [delusion]{moha}, the three appearances: through the siddhas' line of instruction they should ask the lord of the unsurpassed Dharma. The poet claims certain knowledge of the instruction on [innate joy]{sahajananda}, which book-proud yogis lack; Kāṇha's Dohākoṣa agrees (cp.05.m6).

equations.en: crossing the river of great delusion that is the three appearances
the lord of the unsurpassed Dharma
ask (pṛcchatha, second person plural: "you should ask")

citations.quoted: The one path, the innate, is there: Kāṇha knows it clearly. / The lad reads and recites all the many scriptures, and knows nothing at all.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) lacks the request and the mention of innate joy: "kye rnal 'byor pa de'i tshe grub pa'i slob dpon gyi man ngag bdag gis nges par shes so zhes gsungs pa'o", "O yogis, then 'I know for certain the instruction of the siddha master', he said". Everything between the first upadeśa (siddhācāryopadeśa-) and the second (sahajānandopadeśaṃ) is missing, apparently an eye-skip in its source or in translation. In the Tibetan, then, there is no "ask the lord of the unsurpassed Dharma".

yogāspadena caturthapadam āha reads literally "with the ground of yoga he speaks the fourth verse". Munidatta's other openings put the verse in the instrumental and the topic in the accusative (tṛtīyapadena mārgasya anuśaṃsām āhuḥ, cp.05.m5), and the Tibetan "rnal 'byor gyi gnas rkang pa bzhi pas gsungs te" has "with the fourth verse he spoke of the ground of yoga", so I translate as if the text read yogāspadaṃ caturthapadena. āspada may be "ground", "seat" or "footing".

Kāṇha's dohā is corrupt. In "saha ekku pava acchitahiṃ", saha seems to stand for sahaja, "innate"; pava for paha, "path"; and I divide acchi tahiṃ, "is there". The Tibetan "lhan skyes gcig pa'i lam mchog de nyid ni / kAh+Na pa yis gsal bar yongs su shes", "that supreme path of the one innate Kāṇha clearly and fully knows", supports innate, one and path.

vaṭa: I take it as Sanskrit vaṭu (baṭu), "lad, young brahmin pupil", a word also used for a fool; "the fool" is possible. The Tibetan has "lung dang bstan bcos mang po bklags pa dang / sbyangs kyang dbyings pas cung zad shes mi 'gyur", "though he reads and studies many scriptures and treatises, the dbyings pa knows nothing at all"; dbyings pas is unclear, perhaps for byis pas, "the childish".

Other Tibetan differences: "gsal snang gsum gyis rmongs pa chen po'i rtsa", "the channel of great delusion [made] by the three clear appearances", with rtsa, "channel", for nadī, "river" (apparently reading nāḍī); and "de bzhin nyid sgrub pa mi shes", "do not know how to accomplish suchness", for tathāvidhaṃ na jānanti, "do not know it in that way".

questions: cp.05.1a: Munidatta glosses gahana as bhayānaka, "terrifying" (cp.05.m2), and the Tibetan has klong bcas, "with eddies". The draft's "fathomless" overlaps with gambhīra, "deep". Would you like to revisit it? In the commentary I kept the draft's word inside the quotation marks, followed by his gloss.

Names under keep-source: I used Munidatta's own forms as surfaces, [Kṛṣṇācāryapāda]{p-kanha} and [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha}, but normalized the manuscript's Cāṭillapāda to the glossary's Cāṭilapāda (cp.05.m1). Is that the right policy, or should the commentary use the glossary English (Kāṇha, Saraha) throughout?

dharma: in cp.05.m6 I used the surface "Dharma" (capitalized) for "the lord of the unsurpassed Dharma", where the teaching is meant, and lowercase "dharma" in cp.05.m3, where Munidatta means "phenomenon". Should the dharma entry list "Dharma" as a variant?

cp.05.m3: I translate śatrumam as "bridge" (for saṃkramam, which the Tibetan zam pa confirms). Please confirm, and say whether Saraha's corrupt first line should stay as my conjecture "Whoever joins emptiness and compassion" or be marked as uncertain in the rendered edition.

cp.05.m4 and cp.05.m6: at two places I followed a construal the Tibetan supports over the Sanskrit as transmitted ("caught up in sense objects" for vyāvṛti; "with the fourth verse he speaks of the ground of yoga"). The flags give the literal alternatives. Do you accept that?
abhasa: here Munidatta calls "lalanā, rasanā and the rest" the three appearances (cp.05.m2), while in song 14 they are the moon, the sun and the pulinda. Should the abhasa entry record both?

cp.05.m6: the Tibetan loses the instruction to ask the lord of the unsurpassed Dharma, apparently by eye-skip between two occurrences of upadeśa. Is that worth a witness note beside line 5b in the reader edition?
